notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 150, drawn from the sources I was able to access. I have noted where certain traditions or views could not be found.

---

## Overview

Psalm 150 is the closing doxology of the entire Book of Psalms. Each of the five divisions of the Psalter ends with a doxology (Ps 41:13; 72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48), and this whole psalm serves as the finale of the fifth book and the entire collection. The word "praise" (Hebrew *hallel*) appears thirteen times in six verses. The psalm contains no argument or teaching — it is a passionate, eloquent cry to all creation to give Yahweh the praise due to Him.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-150.html

---

## Verse 1

> *Hallelujah! Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him in His mighty heavens.*

**Traditional reading:**

- **"Hallelujah" / "Praise the LORD"**: This psalm shares the same opening and closing line as the preceding four psalms (146–149). No crisis or enemy is in view; this is pure praise. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

- **"Praise God in His sanctuary"**: The sanctuary is the earthly temple — the most fitting place for praise, set apart for God's honour and presence. Gill notes that some rabbis understood this as heaven (God's holy place where angels praise Him), while others understood it as the church below, of which the temple was a type. Gill also notes it could be translated "in His Holy One" and understood of Christ, through whom God is praised. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/150.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary insists the rendering "Praise God in his holiness" (Prayer-book Version) is incorrect — it should be "in his sanctuary," meaning the holy temple. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-150.html

- Ellicott takes "sanctuary" as the earthly temple, noting that — as in Psalm 148 — the invocation to praise includes both heaven and earth, but here in reverse order: the earthly sanctuary first, then the heavens. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/150.htm

- **"Praise Him in His mighty heavens" (firmament of His power)**: The wide expanse of sky — with all its might in storms and weather — is also a fitting place to praise God. Spurgeon: "What an expanse we have in the boundless firmament of divine power! Let it all be filled with praise." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php (excerpt from search)

- Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that under the New Covenant, God's sanctuary is no longer a fixed building in Jerusalem: Jesus serves in a heavenly sanctuary (Heb 8:1–2), makes His sanctuary among His people collectively (2 Cor 6:16) and individually (1 Cor 3:16), and ultimately Jesus Himself will be the sanctuary (Rev 21:22). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

- Spurgeon also notes the shift from "Yah" (in *hallelu-yah*) to "El" (in *halelu-el*) — "Praise God, or the strong God" — linking power with holiness. — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php

---

## Verse 2

> *Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him for His excellent greatness.*

**Traditional reading:**

- **"Praise Him for His mighty acts"**: The first reason for praise. God's mighty acts include creation, providence, deliverance of Israel, and — for the Christian reader — supremely what Jesus accomplished at the cross and empty tomb (Eph 1:19–20). Maclaren renders it "His heroic [or valiant] acts." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

- Gill adds that these mighty acts encompass "the creation of all things out of nothing; the sustaining of all beings; the government of the world; the redemption of man by Christ … the work of grace upon the hearts of his people, and the preservation of them in grace to glory." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/150.htm

- Ellicott sees a structural pairing: "mighty acts" displayed on earth, "excellent greatness" manifested in heaven. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/150.htm

- **"Praise Him according to His excellent greatness"**: A second, deeper reason: praise God not only for what He does but for who He is. The Hebrew can be rendered "the multitude of His greatness" or "muchness of greatness." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-150.html

- Spurgeon: "His being is unlimited, and his praise should correspond therewith. He possesses a multitude or a plenitude of greatness, and therefore he should be greatly praised. There is nothing little about God, and there is nothing great apart from him." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php

- The Pulpit Commentary's homiletic section stresses that praise should answer to "the abundance of his greatness," and not be withheld for daily and hourly loving-kindnesses. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-150.html

---

## Verses 3–5

> *Praise Him with the sound of the horn; praise Him with the harp and lyre. Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and flute. Praise Him with clashing cymbals; praise Him with resounding cymbals.*

**Traditional reading — the orchestra of praise:**

These three verses list the instruments of temple worship. Ellicott calls it a "full orchestra and choir, every kind of instrument known to the Hebrews, wind, string, and percussion, being mentioned." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/150.htm

The instruments include:
- **Trumpet (shophar)**: The curved ram's horn, blown by priests, associated with the giving of the law, the proclamation of jubilee, the coronation of kings, and war. Spurgeon adds it points to Christ's second advent and the resurrection. — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php
- **Harp (kinnor) and lyre (nebel)**: Stringed instruments played by Levites. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/
- **Tambourine (toph)**: A skin stretched over a hoop, like a tambourine, struck by women. Gill notes some render "dance" (machol) as "pipe." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/150.htm
- **Strings (minnim)** and **flute (ugab)**: Minnim literally means "strings put in order"; ugab is likely the syrinx or Pan's pipes. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/
- **Cymbals (tseltselim)**: Two kinds — "loud cymbals" (literally "cymbals of hearing") and "high-sounding/resounding cymbals" (literally "cymbals of tumult"). The Pulpit Commentary notes that cymbals are reserved for last as the instrument most expressive of joy and jubilation, completing the musical climax. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-150.html

**Key interpretive points:**

- The list is not meant to be comprehensive. Boice (cited by Guzik): "The point is actually that everything you have can be used to worship God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

- Maclaren (cited by Guzik) notes that different instruments were played by different classes: the horn by priests, harp and lyre by Levites, timbrels by women dancing — thus, every class and group is to praise God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

- Spurgeon on the trumpet: "Let us never sound a trumpet before us to our own honour, but reserve all our trumpeting for God's glory." On the harp and lyre: "the choicest, the sweetest, must be all our Lord's." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php

- Spurgeon on the timbrel and dance: "Associated with the deliverance at the Red Sea, this form of worship set forth the most jubilant and exultant of worship. The hands and the feet were both employed, and the entire body moved in sympathy with the members." He adds, "There is enough in our holy faith to create and to justify the utmost degree of rapturous delight." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php

- The Pulpit Commentary homiletician (R. Tuck) stresses that "the praise is not in the instrument, but in what the man expresses through the instrument … The most exquisite musical expression is worthless as praise if it is soulless." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-150.html

**DesiringGod (Piper) on vv. 3–5:**

Piper notes that the specific instruments aren't the point — the point is that God deserves more than our words. We praise Him "with our lives — with our decisions, our conversations, our spending, our time" (cf. Rom 12:1). — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-psalms-know-what-you-feel (excerpt from search)

**Gill on the instruments in the Gospel age:**

Gill says these instruments are "not as to be used in Gospel times; but, being expressive of the highest praise and joy shown in former times, are mentioned to set forth the highest strains and notes of praise in New Testament saints; as well as to denote their heartiness, agreement, and unanimity in this service." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/150.htm

---

## Verse 6

> *Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Hallelujah!*

**Traditional reading:**

- This is the climax: the circle widens from the temple congregation to every breathing creature. The literal Hebrew is "Let all breath praise the LORD" (Kidner). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

- Spurgeon: "He gave them breath, let them breathe his praise. His name is in the Hebrew composed rather of breathings than of letters, to show that all breath comes from him: therefore let it be used for him." — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php

- Gill notes that "everything that hath breath" includes not only all people (Jews and Gentiles) but even the brute creatures — though especially spiritual men, converted persons "on whom the Spirit of the Lord has breathed, and whom he has quickened." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/150.htm

- G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik): "The one condition of praise is the possession of breath, that is to say, life received from Him must return in praise to Him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

- The Pulpit Commentary and Guzik both cross-reference Revelation 5:13, where "every creature which is in heaven and on the earth and under the earth … and all that are in them" join in praise to God and the Lamb. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-150.html

- F.B. Meyer (cited by Guzik): "The psalter begins with 'Blessed,' and ends with 'Hallelujah.'" And: "Your life may resemble the psalter with its varying moods, its light and shadow, its sob and smile; but it will end with hallelujahs, if only you will keep true to the will and way and work of the Most Holy." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

- Hengstenberg (cited by Pulpit): "As the life of the faithful, and the history of the Church, so also the Psalter, with all its cries from the depths, runs out in a hallelujah." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-150.html

**Piper (DesiringGod):**

"The purpose of breathing is praise." He says Psalm 150 teaches that God made lungs and vocal cords and oxygen ultimately so that we could use them to worship Him. "Words fall short of his greatness. We feel this when we pray and sing, don't we? It feels true, and yet so inadequate." — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-psalms-know-what-you-feel (excerpt from search)

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ

I was unable to search for specific commentaries from several traditions due to search limits. Here is what I could identify:

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon reads Psalm 150 with characteristic warmth and Christological sensitivity. He sees the trumpet pointing to the second advent, the timbrel and dance recalling Miriam at the Red Sea, and the final verse as a prophecy of the "final triumph of the church of God." His emphasis throughout is that all faculties, talents, and influences must be consecrated to God's praise. — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php

**Reformed Baptist / Reformed evangelical (Piper / DesiringGod):** Piper stresses that Psalm 150 is about responding to God's Word with whole-life praise — not just singing but presenting our bodies as living sacrifices (Rom 12:1). The psalm teaches that "no matter where we are, and how bleak or difficult our life becomes, we always have reason to praise our God." — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-psalms-know-what-you-feel

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (David Guzik / Enduring Word):** Guzik's commentary emphasises loud, joyful, unhesitating praise. Citing Boice: "If you cannot sing loudly and make loud music to praise the God who has redeemed you in Jesus Christ … perhaps it is because you do not really know God or the gospel at all." Guzik highlights the bodily nature of worship (timbrel and dance), though he follows Clarke in suggesting *machol* may mean "pipe" rather than dance. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/

**Divergence on the instruments:** Gill (Baptist, 18th century) explicitly states the instruments are "not as to be used in Gospel times" — they typify spiritual praise only. Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic) treats them as a model of using everything available for worship, with no suggestion they are obsolete. Spurgeon occupies a middle ground: he treats the instruments typologically (the trumpet points to Christ's return, etc.) but also urges readers to "at least let our praise be as decided and bold as if we could give a blast upon the horn." This reflects the historic divide between the Reformed regulative principle of worship (some limiting instruments) and the broader evangelical approach.

- Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/150.htm
- Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-150/
- Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps150.php

**Divergence on who "everything that has breath" addresses:** Ellicott takes a restrictive view: the psalm "so distinctly and positively brings us into the Temple … that we are compelled to see here a hymn specially suited to close the collection of hymns of the covenant … the loud hallelujah … rises from Hebrew voices alone." By contrast, Guzik, Spurgeon, Gill, and the Pulpit Commentary all read it universally — all living creatures everywhere. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/150.htm

## What I could not find

- **Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness** (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com)
- **Lutheran** (lcms.org, 1517.org)
- **Reformed** (ligonier.org, monergism.com) — apart from Piper who is listed on monergism.com
- **Catholic** (newadvent.org, catholic.com)
- **Orthodox** (oca.org)
- **Modern scholarship** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org)
- **The Gospel Coalition** (thegospelcoalition.org)
- **Grace to You / MacArthur** (gty.org)
- **Precept Austin** verse-by-verse specific commentary on Psalm 150 (the site's verse-by-verse tool covers only selected psalms)

The notes above therefore represent primarily the older commentaries (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit), Spurgeon (Baptist), Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic), and Piper (Reformed Baptist), along with the BibleHub summary page.
